summary: A one-page announcement from Raj Reddy at Carnegie Mellon University about a one-day workshop on XCRIBL, a system for producing hard-copy line graphics. CMU had attached a Xerox graphic printer to its PDP-10 using a PDP-11 as a controller. The workshop was set for April 12, and the RFC gives contacts for details and local arrangements.

eli5.summary: A school says it built a special machine that draws pictures on paper. It invites other people to come for a day, see how it works, and learn how to use it.

subtitle: Workshop on hard-copy line graphics at Carnegie Mellon University

tldr.problem: Standard computer line printers could not produce variable-width fonts or graphics—they could only print fixed-width characters.
tldr.mechanism: Carnegie Mellon University interfaced a Xerox Graphic Printer (XGP) to their PDP-10 computer using a PDP-11 as an intelligent controller, allowing the system to generate printing instructions dynamically rather than pre-computing a full page image.
tldr.outcome: The XCRIBL system produced documents with multiple typefaces, line graphics, and gray-scale images. CMU held a workshop on April 12, 1972 to teach other sites how to use it.

today: RFC 320 announces Carnegie Mellon's XCRIBL workshop in March 1972. It represents early work in digital typography and high-quality document printing—technologies that would become central to modern publishing and computer graphics.

sections.title: The Xerox Graphic Printer Interface
sections.content: Carnegie Mellon's Computer Science Department built an interface between its PDP-10 computer and a Xerox Graphic Printer (XGP) (a modified facsimile copying machine), using a PDP-11 as an intelligent controller. The XGP works like a photocopier but uses a cathode ray tube similar to a television as the light source instead of reflected light. The system has been working since January 1972.
sections.eli5: A computer controls a special Xerox machine that can draw anything, not just type regular letters.

sections.title: How the XCRIBL System Works
sections.content: The XCRIBL system draws an image as a series of dots on the CRT with a resolution of 12 dots per inch. These dots are reflected onto a selenium drum, which electrostatically attracts a fine black powder to the exposed areas. The powder is transferred to moving paper and fused in place by heat. Instead of requiring the computer to generate a complete bit image of the entire page in memory, the system generates each scan line as needed, using special data structures and a character set design program that lets operators easily design and modify character sets in a grid on a display terminal.
sections.eli5: The system draws dots in rows on a special drum, which then prints them on paper. You can design your own letters by editing them on a screen.

sections.title: Capabilities and the April 12 Workshop
sections.content: The XGP can print documents with any typeface, not the fixed fonts of ordinary printers. It can also draw lines and gray-scale images—the AI group used it to print pictures of faces and speech spectrograms. CMU held a one-day workshop on April 12, 1972 at Carnegie Mellon to teach other sites how to use XCRIBL. The morning covered document generation languages and systems; the afternoon covered character set generation, the PDP-11 support system, and hardware interface details. Evening sessions were reserved for open discussion of unsolved problems. Attendees could stay at the Webster Hall Hotel or Civic Center Motor Hotel, within walking distance of the university.
sections.eli5: The system can print fancy letters and pictures. CMU offered a day-long class on how to use it, with time to ask questions in the evening.
